newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to act in German bank row if Kohl move fails.
newsitem.headline: EU to act in German bank row if Kohl move fails.

text.p: The European Commission is reluctant to enter a dispute between German private and state banks but is likely to do so if Bonn fails to shield the public Landesbanken from EU competition rules, Commission and banking officials say.
The long-standing dispute, in which commercial banks accuse their rivals of distorting competition due to public support, has always been highly sensitive and political, the sources noted.
It became even more so with a recent proposal by the German government to exclude banks from European Union treaty provisions banning public subsidies which harm fair competition.
The proposal was made within the framework of the inter-governmental conference (IGC) to reform the EU treaty ahead of the bloc's expansion eastwards.

This and a string of other proposals, including whether to keep the Commission at bay on the issue of public funding for state-controlled television broadcasters, will be decided at a summit of EU leaders in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.

Any revision of the treaty requires the unanimous approval of all 15 states, a difficult obstacle but one which Commission officials are cautious not to overestimate given a long tradition of EU horse-trading sessions when new treaties are negotiated.
"Obviously we are very concerned by (the German proposal)," European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told Reuters on Tuesday while refusing to comment any further.

German private banks complained to the Commission in 1994 about the transfer of 11 billion marks of capital from state housing development agencies to the publicly-owned regional banks or Landesbanken.
The Landesbanken do not offer retail banking but compete with private banks in corporate finance, securities trading and issuing.
WestLB, the biggest of all and the country's third largest bank, received four billion marks in fresh equity capital on its own.

The Commission's competition services have long concluded that there were enough grounds for starting formal proceedings, which would require the Bonn government to defend itself and allow banks elsewhere in the EU to file formal comments, but the issue is currently blocked at a higher level, the sources said.
"We have the treaty. We know what to do but reality is another thing," an EU source said. "It all depends on the decision of the hierarchy."

One thing is sure. The Commission will not act until it sees how the other 14 EU states react to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's proposal. But if Kohl fails, it will start a formal probe, although nobody would venture when this could happen.
Banking officials said that banks in other EU countries, not just Germany, felt strongly about the Landesbanken.
French credit institutions, in particular, had voiced concern about WestLB's incursion in northern France but it was not clear how the new Socialist government would react.

The Commission's shyness in the German banking dispute highlights its limitations to clamp down on public subsidies, especially when powerful national governments are involved, and nowhere is this more visible than with Germany.
This is the second time Kohl has stepped in to try to stop the Commission acting on this and a related issue, the sources said.

Although the Commission was only asked to rule on the 11 billion marks transferred to the Landesbanken since 1990, the fight also hinges on the issue of unlimited German government guarantees to public banks which rule out the possibility of such banks being liquidated and ensure full protection to all creditors.

The Commission has been trying for years to introduce some discipline in the field of public guarantees given mostly to ailing state-controlled industry and banks, particularly to help them find financing at a reduced cost. The practice is also widespread in Italy and France.

But the sources said a draft communication warning banks that guarantees may be declared illegal if not previously cleared by the Commission had also been put on hold for about a year after Kohl's personal intervention.
